[18] 20230612_182121.jpg

Type of Draw — Number of Outs — Example

Gutshot: 4 outs. 9♥-8♦ on A♥-6♦-5♣.

Open-ended straight draw: 8 outs. 9♥-8♦ on A♥-7♦-6♣.

Flush draw: 9 outs. K♥-Q♥ on A♥-7♥-6♣.

Set to full house: 7–10 outs. 7♣-7♥ on 7♦-4♦-2♦.

Gutshots are far more important than most people realize. Due to their disguised nature they can, in the right situations, generate tremendous value from implied odds. Open-ended straight draws have twice as many outs but they aren’t as well disguised and can also be duplicated. Flush draws are very powerful, especially nut flush draws, since they can’t be duplicated.

Finally, board pair outs can come in handy if you hold a set and run into a straight or flush. If this happens on the the flop, you will have seven outs to pair the board on the turn. If you miss your draw on the turn, you will have ten outs to improve on the river regardless of which turn card is dealt.

The dynamic nature of each draw will become more apparent later in the book. Below is a chart of outs and the odds of improving when you hold this number of outs. Don’t worry about memorizing all of these numbers. There will be a simple formula for this in the next section.

Rule of Two and Four

If memorizing these charts seems like a daunting task, have no worries. There’s a much easier way to quickly estimate how likely you are to improve. If you’re on the flop, count up all your outs and multiply by four. If you’re on the turn, count up all your outs and multiply by two.

Rule of Two (for turn play)

(number of outs)(2) = odds of improving

Example for straight draw (8 outs)

(number of outs)(2) = odds of improving

(8)(2) = odds of improving

16% = odds of improving

[20] 20230612_182134.jpg

Rule of Four (for flop play)

(number of outs)(4) = odds of improving

Example for flush draw (9 outs) (number of outs)(4) = odds of improving (9)(4) = odds of improving 36% = odds of improving

Bear in mind that the Rule of Four has a maximum absolute error of 3% up to 12 outs. The Rule of Two is slightly less accurate as the number of outs increases. If you're looking for an even more accurate way to estimate your odds of improving, use the modified formula below.

Modified Rule of Two (for turn play)

(number of outs)(2) + [(number of outs)(2)]/10 = odds of improving

Example for flush draw (9 outs) (9)(2) + {(9)(2))/10 = odds of improving 48 + 18/10 = odds of improving 48 + 1.8 = odds of improving 19.8% = odds of improving

All you're doing is calculating your odds of improving using the first formula and then adding 10% of that number. This formula has a maximum absolute erro! of less than 0.9% for up to 19 outs. Below is a modified version of the Rule ° Four. The original formula is accurate up to nine outs. However, when it comes ©

more accurate formula for draws with ten or more outs.

[21] 20230612_182137.jpg

Modified Rule of Four (for river play with 10+ outs)

(number of outs)(3) + 9 = odds of improving

Example for a combo draw with 15 outs (15)(3) + 9 = odds of improving 45 + 9 = odds of improving 54% = odds of improving.

This formula has a maximum absolute error of less than 1% for up to 19 outs. So now you have a great system to quickly double-check your odds of improving. Use this technique in every hand you play.

Backdoor Equity

There are 2,162 turn and river permutations on any given flop. If the order that the turn and river are dealt doesn’t matter, there are really only 1,081 permutations. It’s pretty easy to figure this out. By the time the flop is dealt, your two hole cards and the three cards on the flop are visible.

If you subtract the five visible cards from a deck of 52 cards, you realize that there are 47 unseen cards. One of those cards has to be dealt on the turn. After the turn is dealt, one of the remaining 46 cards must be dealt on the river. 47 x 46 = 2,162. If the order of these cards doesn’t matter, you just divide by two to find the total number of turn and river permutations. 2,162/2 = 1,081.

Below is a list of backdoor draws and the equities associated with them. These percentages my seem small, but they can have a tremendously profitable impact on your global strategy if implemented correctly. Thus, they are included in this section.

[22] 20230612_182151.jpg

“impact that they can have on your turn equity, will play a considerable role in the aggressive strategy that we will examine.

Diluted Equity

Before we end our pot equity discussion, there's one final thing you need to ‘know. When draws clash with certain holdings, their equities can become 2 ‘little diluted. It's important for you to be aware of this phenomenon and react accordingly.

board pairs on the river.

[23] 20230612_182154.jpg

Flush Draw versus Set

The same concept applies when a flush draw collides with a set. Typically, a flush draw will improve to a flush 36% of the time (9 outs x 4 = 36%). However, that doesn’t mean it will improve to the best hand. The board could pair on the turn leaving you drawing dead. You could also rnake your hand on the turn, only to lose when the board pairs on the river.

Flush Draw versus Set (No Blockers)

The worst situation is when the board pairs and completes a flush simultaneously. This situation is rare but it comes up from time to time. In a nutshell, it’s best to subtract 6-9% equity from your draw if you think you're up against a set.

Pot Odds

Consideration of pot odds is just like any other form of wagering. You evaluate how much you are risking in comparison to the reward. Then you evaluate how often you expect to reap the reward. A disparity between the ratios will result in long-term gains or losses.

I'm a very visual learner. When I'm trying to visualize pot odds | just ask myself, “If | call, what percentage of the total pot will my call be?” Then limagine a pie chart such as the one below. That’s how often | need to have the best hand to break even on the call.

implied Odds

Considering pot odds allows you to evaluate risk versus reward on one street. implied odds evaluate risk versus reward for multiple streets. You can often make a call on an early street that is not getting the correct outright pot odds. However, you do it because you think you can induce your opponent to make 2 mistake on a later street when you make your draw.

For example, let's say the pot is $100. Effective stacks are $1,000. Tne board is A-Q-7-6. You have 5-4. You know Villain has A-A. Villain bets $100. At this point your are getting 2-to-1 on your call. You need to improve to the best hand 33% of the time to breakeven if the hand ends on the turn, After studyiNg Pot equity, you know that your open-ended straight draw will only improve © the best hand 20% of the time. Clearly, if the hand ended on the turn you shoul fold. However, there is still another street to play.

sake of simplicity, let's say you know th win Villa! ‘ast $900 on the occasions you make your straight. A simple evaluation of pos sible outcomes causes you to realize that this is a very profitable situation.

Four times out of five you will call $100, miss your straigTM draw, and fold the river. Total loss: $400.

One time out of five you will make your straight and stack your

opponent. You will profit $200 (Villain’s stack). ove vitternre turn Det

Plus the pot ($100), while recoveri investmen Total profit: $1,100.

ADVANCED Cane

[27] 20230612_182217.jpg

if you take your total losses ($400) and subtract them from your

total profits ($1,100), you see that you are earning $700 in five possible outcomes. If you take your net ($700) and divide it by the total

number of outcomes (5), you see that you're averaging a $140 profit

each time you make the call on the turn.

Clearly, this is a great situation for you. Now you understand the power of implied odds. This phenomenon can be expressed in a simple forrnula.

EV = (% make draw)(average net profit) - (% missed draw)(call)

Let's use the example from the paragraph above.

EV = (0.2)($1,100) - (0.8)($100) EV = $220 - $80 EV = $140

EV stands for “expected value.” It simply means how much you expect to win Or lose on average each time you make a particular play. Notice that the equation is really simple. The tough part is accurately figuring out how much money You can expect to make on average when you make your hand. There are just \Way too many variables to ever know the exact amount you can expect to win. This is where experience comes into play. It’s just part of developing an intuitive Understanding of the game.

Dynamic Fold Equity

Semi-bluffs rely on dynamic fold equity. The purpose of dynamic fold equity calculations is to determine how often your opponent needs to fold for you to breakeven if you're semi-bluffing with a draw. Again, this is similar to pot odds calculations except you're the one making the bet.

ae you evaluate porn you are risking in comparison to the reward. Then you evaluate how often you expect to reap the reward. A disparity between the ratios will result in long-term gains or losses.

“ween the ratios withtesure ks Sie Eff ‘al

skim these equations.

Advanced Fold Equity Equation

EV = XP + (1-X)(WH-LV) X = folding frequency P = pot size W = amount won (net profit)

ADVANCED

[31] 20230612_182250.jpg

H = our equity, also (1-V) L = amount lost V = opponent(s) equity, also (1-H)

This is the same way Derric Heynie describes fold equity in his book Quantum Poker: Summing Up Everything You will Ever Need to Know About Poker. To solve the example above, all we need to do is input the variables and estimate how often Villain is folding. Let's say we think Villain is folding 40% of the time.

X = folding frequency = 40% or 0.4 P = pot size = $100 W = net profit = $200 H = our equity = 20% or 0.2 L = amount lost = $100 V = opponent(s) equity = 80% or 0.8

EV = XP + (1-X)(WH-LV)

EV = (0.4)(100) + (1 - 0.4) [(200)(0.2) - (100)(0.8)] EV = 40 + 0.6 (40 - 80) EV = 40 + 0.6 (-40) EV = 40 + (-24) EV = 16

On average you will profit $16 each time you shove if your opponent is folding 40% of the time. Now let me explain how we find the breakeven point. We simply change the expected value from the last equation to zero and solve for X.

0 = XP + (1-X)(WH-LV)

O= (X)(100) + (1-x)[(200)(0.2) - (100)(0.8)] 0 = 100x + (1-X)(40 - 80) 0 = 100X + (1-X)(-40) 0 = 100X - 40 + 40X 40 = 100X + 40X 40 = 140X

[32] 20230612_182307.jpg

140X = 40 X = 40/140 x=4/14 X = 0.29 or 29% As I said, you only need your opponent to fold 29% of the time to Make profit in this situation. That's the power of the semi-bluff. Now before you Panic there's an easier way to solve these equations. Simply go over to redchippoke, com/fold-equity-calculator/ and use their semi-bluff calculator. You simply en. ter the four known variables into the calculator and let it solve for fold equity Later, you will realize how how extremely valuable a fold equity calculator is tc your poker development. Again, this is a situation where running the numbers away from the table will have a dramatic effect on your play at the table.

Then, if you're uncertain of what {to do, you can always revert to an unexploitable range until you gather more information on your opponent. It also helps to boost your confidence and avoid thoughts of uncertainty when you're on a downswing.

There are a few things that you should always consider before puttin chips in the pot pre-flop. They are fundamental principles — things that at always true. Together they will generate almost 100% of the profits that yo

Card edge is the most important. Having an equity advantage and/0! ® playability advantage versus your opponent's range is what it’s all about. That goes hand in hand with initiative. Being the last pre-flop aggressor uncaps y ou range, allowing you to represent hands that your opponent cannot have, thus improving your ability to generate fold equity.

Position is also important but it doesn’t have nearly as much value witho" initiative. A strong range with initiative can easi itional 0” advantage. The same goes for skill ed Be

adds value to card edge, initiative, and position.

Allow me to explain.

[45] 20230612_182429.jpg

We all know limping is unprofitable. Every poker coach tells you not to do it. But they don’t offer much of an explanation. At most, they say you want to ‘put pressure on the big blind. But that can’t be the only issue, To further understand, all you have to do is ask yourself a few questions.

Do you have a card edge? If you do you should have raised for value. Do you have initiative? No. You forfeited it by limping. [Do you have position? Very rarely. You're always exposed to an isolation raise. [Do you have a skill edge? Even if you do, you're fighting an uphill battle.

Flatting weak broadway hands versus tight opening ranges is just as bad. OWGFten do you see a nit open UTG with a tight range like 9-9+/A-Q+ and get flatted by a hand like K-100? This is one of the easiest ways to burn money.

(Do'you have a card edge? No. You're at an equity and playability disadvantage.

‘Do you have initiative? No. You forfeited it by flatting.

DoVou have position? Yes. But it isn’t nearly as valuable without initiative.

§DSVeU have a skill edge? Even if you do you're fighting an uphill

battle. Lastly, flatting small pocket pairs versus loose opening ranges is a leak that Nobody cares to patch. How often do you see a wannabe Viktor Blom open 50% of hands from late position and get flatted by pocket deuces from the ‘small blind? This is a very slow, miserable death. Again...

disadvantage.

hand pre-flop.

Uncapping Your Range

This often caps your range, meaning that it will be much more difficult for ‘you to Pepesent @ strong range of hands post-flop. Limping is often done because your hand is too weak to raise for value because you're in early position and will likely have to play the remainder of the hand out of position.

It'sa very slippery slope. You simply lack every pre-flop edge. Flatting isn’t fhuch better. When you flat you are essentially acknowledging that your range isinherently weaker than Villain’s range. Again, you're sacrificing card edge, inifiative, and frequently position. Can your skill edge really overcome all of that?

[Have you ever wondered why you check to the pre-flop aggressor? You intuitively know that checking is almost always better than leading out when Youldon't have the pre-flop initiative. But why? Have you ever stopped to con- Siderthe dynamics of this decision?

S'because you acknowledged that Villain had a stronger range than you Whenlyou flatted. It’s very easy to extrapolate on this by evaluating basic flop fextuires) Consider a flop of J-6-2r. It’s unlikely that either of you have connected with this board.

time, if you're lucky enough to make a pair, you know that more value by checking than by betting. Why? Because, as Villain will c-bet this board over 70% of the time. When you ‘know that you can get at least one street of value over 70% of the time by ‘checking, you have little incentive to bet.

Betting could induce Villain to fold many of his weak holdings. Each time folds, you miss an opportunity to induce him to bluff. This why you should be more likely to slowplay a set ona dry flop. Why check-raise when Villain is unlikely to have anything that can call? ‘Instead, you're much better off calling and attempting to induce a second bet from Villain.

But what happens when you don’t check-raise your strong hands on dry

02 - Pre-Flop Play

[48] 20230612_182458.jpg

flops? It means you probably don’t have anything the times that you check-raise. This makes it difficult for you to check-raise as a bluff. It also means that Villain can bet over 70% of his hands and get away with it. Villain c-bets and you’re often forced to fold when you miss. He can bet with impunity and you can’t really do anything to change that. Truly, the only incentive you have to flat out of position is pot odds.

I say ‘usually’ because this is where the power of position comes into play. It’s easy to think that all you have to do is estimate Villain’s stealing range, plug that into a pre-flop equity calculator, and compare that equity to your pot odds. The problem is that you won’t always be able to realize all of your equity by flatting.

Pre-flop equity calculators assume that you will see all five cards. But now you know that you will rarely see all five cards since I’ve established that Villain can bet over 70% of his range with impunity on most boards. Consider the times you defend with a hand like 8-7o on the same board of J-6-2r. You check, Villain bets, and you have nothing so you fold.

You lost an opportunity to make a pair against a hand like K-Q. You also lost an opportunity for the turn and river to run out 10-9, 9-5, 5-4, 8-8, 7-7, or 8-7 against a hand like A-J. You missed these opportunities because by flatting you acknowledged that your range was weaker than Villain’s range. This all leads back to my initial point. Flatting is bad and limping is worse. So always consider the four ways that you can create profit pre-flop: card edge, skill edge, position, and initiative.

After finishing an AAS in Paramedic Technology – most of which was at a Level I trauma center – I’m now used to things like protocols, guidelines, quality assurance programs, and decentralized command concepts. It’s easy to get distracted by a broken leg while someone is going into cardiac arrest. You have to prioritize.

Protocols are for situations that come up frequently. Guidelines are for situations on the fringe of protocols. Quality assurance programs are for developing the critical thinking skills necessary to solve problems outside the protocols and guidelines.

Did you notice how Snowie isn’t fist-pumping to open 10-10 from EP1? Here’s the bottom line: The blinds are your only financial incentive to open preflop. In other words, if the blinds didn’t exist you would have no incentive to play a hand from EP1. You would have incentive to move all-in with A-A from other positions if someone put chips in the pot. But other than that, you would have no incentive to play a hand.

ou ask your an

¢ Does Villain ever limp with malicious intent? By that | mean, does he ever limp intending to raise with a big hand? This is a common tactic that can throw a wrench into a loose-aggressive isolation strategy. You must seek to identify and exploit these players. bses Villain limp-calll or limp-fold as a default? You can iso- Jate much wider than normal against a player who limp-folds as a default. However, you need to inject more value into your isolation range against someone that limp-calls as a default. you can’t answer these questions you should operate off of these two leyassumptions until proven otherwise...

Without info, assume that Villain has no malicious intentions. It's uncommon to run into a limp-raiser. It’s rare to run into a Villain Who limp-raises as a bluff. Assume that Villain is only limp-raising with monsters until proven otherwise. ithout info, assume that Villain will limp-call with most o J Fange. Make sure that your isolation range has enough Vo"

[62] 20230612_182630.jpg

+ Asadefault, isolate to your normal opening size plus one big bj, per limper. So if you normally open to 3.5bb, you should Slate one limper by raising to 4.5bb, and two limpers Dy raising to 5.5bh As a default, isolate one limper with the top 75% of your Opening range from each position. So if you normally open with 36% of hands on the button, you should isolate one limper with 27% of

your range. Asa default, isolate two limpers with the top 50% of your opening range from each position. So if you normally open with 36% of hands on the button, you should isolate two limpers with 18% of your range. As a default, isolate three or more limpers with a range of 9-9+/ A-Q+. It’s important to inject value into situations where you will most likely have to go post-flop in a bloated, multiway pot. When in doubt, tight is right when isolating three or more limpers. As a default, never over-limp from a position earlier than the cutoff. It’s important to minimize the chances of getting isolated by someone behind you. It’s too difficult to fight back out of position with a capped range. As a default, it’s okay to over-limp with small pocket Pairs, suited connectors, and suited gappers against weak opponents. But it’s important to avoid over-limping with weak Broadway hands. You need to be able to retain your equity on later streets,

‘gx BIN Open — BB Defense

‘There are two key differences between defending from the big blind and ‘defending from the small blind. In the small blind, you're getting a bad price with big blind action pending, In the big blind, you're getting a good price and ‘YOU can close the action, As a result, you have much less incentive to 3-bet

from the big blind.

3x CO Open — BB Defense

Optimal cutoff opens are significantly tighter than optimal button opens. A few major alterations need to be made to your big blind defense range.

Eliminate the A-2 - A-50 S-bets (you wan't be able to generate enough fold equity against a tighter range)

Eliminate the suited gappers (I know they look pretty, but they

won't hold-up against three barrels from a solid opponent) Eliminate the weaker suited K-x hands (kicker issues are Magnified against tighter ranges).

All of this is, of course, assuming that the cutoff is opening at an optimal frequency. If he’s opening a button range, go back to a wider defense range 3-bet more liberally, and create some chaos!

[76] 20230612_182747.jpg

3-betting light is a much less viable option against early and middle position opens. Early position openers have to deal with so many players behind them — players who can wake up with a hand and 3-bet, or flat and force the opener to play three streets out of position — that they have no choice but to tighten their opening ranges. Consequently, it’s difficult to generate fold equity by 3-betting light against their value-centric ranges.

[80] 20230612_182810.jpg

Defending from the Small Blind

What happens when you flat out of the small blind?

You imply that your range is weaker and less playable than Villain’s You surrender the initiative, thus capping your range and making it much more difficult to generate fold equity post-flop. You agree to play the rest of the hand out of position and you forfeit residual equity to Villain’s c-bets. You handcuff your skill edge by making it much more difficult to generate fold equity and actualize residual equity. You forfeit 12-24% more equity with overcards and you allow Villain to actualize 12-24% more equity with overcards. You give the big blind a great price to call and dilute your equity. You give the big blind an opportunity to squeeze and force you to forfeit 100% of your pre-flop investment.

What happens when you 3-bet from the small blind?

You imply that your range is stronger and more playable than Villain’s range.

You claim the initiative, thus uncapping your range, making it much easier to generate fold equity post-flop. You are less likely to play the rest of the hand out of position, and you force Villain to forfeit residual equity to your esau a unleash your skill edge by making it much easier to generate fold equity and actualize residual equity, sa suliniae tl 2-24% more equity with overcards, and you force Villain to forfeit 12-24% more equity with overcards.

equity while simultaneous creating 1bb wart af dead money. Speco tk costly for the big blind to 4-bet, thus retaining more of your equity.

Which option sounds better?

There are only two situations where | don't 3-bet my entire continuance range out of the small blind. This first one is in multi-way pots. 3-Betting

in virtually every poker variant with community cards, y . tO inflate the

size of the pot in position. It’s fundamental game theory. In Limit Hold'em, Voy basically never enter a hand without raising. In Pot Limit Omaha, you relent. lessly isolate all the limpers with any playable hand when stacks are deep |, Pot Limit Omaha Eight or Better, you relentlessly isolate all the limpers wit, almost every A-2-x-x combo. In Pineapple, you 3-bet almost every suite A-x-x combo because people are so unwilling to stack off with K-K-x combos, it's no different in No Limit Hold’em!

don’t know why people love flatting the button so much. In fact, I'm so glad Daniel Negreanu wrote Power Hold’em Strategy and perpetuated this “small ball” poker nonsense, because he's one of the only players in the world who can hand read well enough to make that strategy work. Everyone else gets crushed. Take a look at any online grinder’s PokerTracker 4 or Hold'em Manager 2 database and | quarantee that you will not find one person making money by flatting the button wider than 12% of the time — not one!

You have to 3-bet in position to claim the initiative, imply that you have a range advantage, and unleash your skill edge. You will always gather more information by betting and raising than you will by checking and calling. Poker is a war fought with imperfect information! Why are you inhibiting your ability to gather information by flatting the button?

‘mm going to teach you how to play poker like a grown up. I've successfully implemented this strategy at every level up to $10-$25NL. I'm sure it would work in bigger games too. The only problem is that bigger games don't really run anymore so | don't have enough of a sample size to Prove it

kle up! You're going to learn so INgs In the upcomin just remember that it’s one thing to understand the theory and talk a bi aeeg It’s a totally different thing pulling the trigger.

4-Betting

4-betting is an underutilized maneuver in live games because nobody is 3-bey,

ace high.” The only reason I’m showing you this sty is So you know what to do against tough opponents.

The idea is to really polarize your range between K-K+/A-K and A-x block. ers that you can’t defend with profitably. You need to 4-bet light just enough that Villain has to start giving you action with Q-Q/J-J/A-K. Now obviously, if Villain is literally never 3-betting light, you should never 4-bet light. It’s just that simple.

Now there's one more caveat to all of this: stack size. The deeper you ale, the lighter you should 3-bet and 4-bet because Villain has to risk more to put you all-in. The shorter you are the tighter you should 3-bet and 4-bet because once Villain is all-in the hand is over and you can no longer re-steal if he's light

‘So, a the most extreme circumstance (short stack tournament poker): you should never 3-bet light with more than about 25% of your range. If you 3-bet lighter than that Villain could literally shove with any two cards and be profitable in the long term (think about fold equity).

n the flip side, if you're eep, you could liter - ith every combo of A-2 - A-50, and dare Villain to 5-bet knowing that youre still free to 6-bet all-in. Ideally, you want to 4-bet to about 20% of effective tacks without giving Villain a great pf - This crea = mendous amount of leverage by risking 20% af your stack (at Most) to force Villain to risk his entire stack if he believes you're 4-betting light.

Humans learn by trial and error and assume that what- Ver works jg “optimal”. Snowie is disproving many of our preconceived biases ith extremely advanced artificial intelligence.

3x CO Open — BTN 3-Bet + CO 4-Bet (Pot)

The button’s 3-betting range should be much wider than the small blind’s 3-betting range because he has absolute position. Therefore, the cutoff should be 4-betting with 10-10+/A-K to force out the button’s equity.

Also, did you notice how conservative Snowie's defense range is? It’s not looking to play many pots out of position, especially against Digger 3-bets. Just like last hand, if the cutoff was min-raising, the button would 3-bet smaller, and the cutoff would be able to call much wider, because the stack-to-pot ratio would be much larger. This is all fundamental game theory that you must absorb.

3x HJ Open — CO 3-Bet — BTN 4-Bet (1/2-pot)

This is where Snowie is really good at crushing people with brute force. It’s cold 4-betting a ton in a situation where both opponents have no choice but to shove or fold. It’s basically saying, “| have A-A and if you don’t believe me, ou can stick 100bb in light.” Live p averse that I've a. to-cold 4-betting A-2 - A-5s from the button for years. | thought | was doing it exploitatively. It turns out this is optimal!

3x CO Open —+ BTN 3-Bet + CO 4-Bet > BTN 5-Bet [Part 1] (All-in)

The button should be 3-betting so wide that the cutoff should be 4-betting with 10-10+/A-K and enough random bluffs that the button can profitably 5-bet shove J-J+/A-K when you consider fold equity. Snowie is very rarely flatting with 100bb. As I said earlier, you want to force the Villain to surrender all of his equity or inflate the size of the pot when you have an equity advantage.

There's one last thing that | want to point out before we move on. If you choose to use a larger sizing in the previous example, then something very interesting happens at the 200bb stack depth. [121] 20230612_183027.jpg

‘squeezing from the Big Bling

ui a) blind in multi-way pots. Firstly, there’ 4 f “ipl 7 ones 9 type. Secondly, there’s the ~. aha middle around is the nath ta fallau “gance, the middle ground is the path to follow.

Just lke defending aut of the big blind in heads-up pots, the only reason yutave to defend out of position is good pot odds. Why else would you sac- ‘fice card edge, position, and initiative? The only difference is that the odds you're getting are now significantly better.

if the button raises 3x and the small blind flats, you're getting 7-to- 2 on your call. Once again, it’s easy to think that all you need to do is figure out which hands have 22% equity versus the combined ranges of the button and small blind. Almost every hand in your range has that much equity! But does that mean you should defend with everything?

No. You won't always be able to see turns and rivers. Many times, the small dling will check, you'll check and the button will c-bet, forcing you to checkfold residual amounts of equity.

As a result, it’s important to ask yourself how much equity you'll be able to “pture with each hand in your range. Suited A-x and K-x hands, small pocket Me Suited connectors, and suited gappers capture the most equity. Focus on those hands!

Resist the urge to peel with weak, offsuit, disjointed hands like A-30, K-50

able hands for miserable grinders:

Nd. This works as follows:

[122] 20230612_183035.jpg

3x BTN Open — SB Call + BB Defense

You should call and 3-bet much wider and with a different composition of hands, when the small blind is the flatter. The button is Opening a wide range of hands and the small blind is out of position with a capped range (mostly small pairs and weak Broadways). Suited connectors play very well in position, in 3-bet pots, against small pairs and weak Broadways.

Flat with suited A-x and K-x hands, suited gappers, and Suited double-gappers. These hands are now playable because the pot odds you're getting have improved significantly. That being said, they arent great for Squeezing against the small blind’s pocket pair heavy range. Call with them and outperform the small blind in position.

3x CO Open — BTN Call + BB Defense

Snowie is 3-betting 6-6+ versus an optimal 3x cutoff open and butto" flat. Intuitively, | think this is too wide against human Opponents. Humans tend

[125] 20230612_183047.jpg

.reezing from the

“fest Jacking card edge, skill edge, Position, and initiative. Now it’s even festa you're out of position against multiple Opponents.

squeezing is So much better, especially since live players tend to open too ie fat too wide, and call 3-bets too wide. This is not a bad thing for your weaker holdings. In fact, it increases their profitability!

loose-passive players are great at building bigger pots for you to win on jeter streets. You just have to be willing to fire extra barrels to capitalize on their passivity.

Many of my students get a little gun-shy when they squeeze with A-5s and get called by the button. They c-bet the flop, the button calls, and they surrender. They‘re uncomfortable firing big semi-bluffs. | have to remind them constantly that their opponents are even more uncomfortable calling big bets, with weak holdings, against a player who clearly has a range advantage!

Long gone are the days where you could peel with speculative holdings and Slack novice players. All those guys went broke ten years ago. The remaining Payers are the nits who won because they refused to go broke with one pair. atch them play long sessions all day, every day passing money back an orth.

‘hat to the max.

3x CO Open — BTN Call + SB 3-Bet

Flatting with 7-7 - 9-9 is fine, especially if there's a fish in the big blind. You could also flat some weaker hands such as K-Js or A-Qo if the button '5 very splashy. Other than that, you should be 3-betting big and planning 0" firing multiple barrels. It's the only way to win nowadays,

Good luck trying to flat K-100 out of position against two solid players. 3x HJ Open — CO Call — SB 3-Bet

What eventually starts to happen here is all the scared money at the table starts min-raising the flop with top pair trying to end the hand early. Thats even better because it allows you to play with virtual clairvoyance. You ca" give up with gutshots and pile in with combo draws.

Then, the times that they call, they usually have some sort of draw or middle-pair-plus-gutshot type hand. The maximal exploit against this range is to overbet all blank rivers. It’s very counter-intuitive. Typically, you want the river to favor your range, but against this type of player it doesn't matter.

Before we begin, there are two very important notes | need to Make Firstly, the hand history graphics in the following pages display the true pot size at all times. However, the text below the graphics occasional assumes a $5-$15 rake to simplify the math for novice players. Moreover you should assume that all stack sizes are 100bb unless specifically noted There are a couple of situations where | deliberately changed the stack depth to illustrate how the stack-to-pot ratio can change the profitability of common lines. You'll soon see why.

Objectives

You'll remember that we previously analyzed pre-flop play and devised 2 methodology, involving a series of typical questions that you need to ask yourself pre-flop. The same methodology will serve you very well postflop and the typical questions to ask are as follows,

For all post-flop situations

What is the pot size? What are the stack sizes? What is the stack-to-pot ratio? What is the board? Who has a range advantage? Who has a capped range? Who has an uncapped range?

Who benefits the most from turns and rivers? Who is my opponent? Is he tired? Is he tilted? Why?

Post-flop, out of position, without initiative

How often does Villain c-bet ? What price am | getting? What price do | need to continue? How often does he double-barrel? How often does he triple-barrel? How often does he overbet?

How often does he fold to check-raises? How often does he check behind? What does he check behind with? Is his checking range too capped? Should | lead out?

Should | overbet turns if the flop checks through?

Did you notice how each section included more and more questions’ That's because the sections are ranked from best to worst. You're almost always better off being in position with initiative. You will always gain To® information by betting and raising than you will by checking and calling. Being out of position without the initiative only increases the complexity of the hand reading process.

There may be a few concepts listed that people are unfamiliar with The most Eermon 6 Eapiecting your checking range. It’s important to ‘ail derstand this idea. Many players open pre-flop, get called by the big blind, and then check behind on the flop with weak showdown value hands. They never check with stronger hands to protect the weaker ones. As a cons quence, they're very easy to exploit on turns and rivers.

\t’s important to think in terms of ranges and Tange advantages. This will guide you through the various different situations that can arise. Heads-UP pots are much more dynamic than multi-way pots. There's a lot Bare room to maneuver and adapt to maximally exploit Villain, Multi-way pots require Tice more honesty, and there's nothing wrong with that.

Hero bets $100. He is risking $100 to win $200. He needs Villain :, fold 33% of the time to break even. Villain has to defend 67% of the time to prevent Hero from profitably bluffing with any two cards. Hero bet the river assuming that Villain would fail to meet minimum defense frequency

[139] 20230612_183207.jpg

takes a lot of the guesswork out of poker. sure, there will still be situations where it’s a close call. However, the “ere majority of the time, if you think it’s close between val- “yeetting and checking, you should bet for value. People leave so much ‘value on the table. You only need to get called by a worse hand 51% of ‘the time, lf you're not occasionally getting called by better, you're doing something wrong!

The same goes for situations where you think it’s close between bluffjing and checking. The overwhelming majority of the time, if you think it’s dose) You should close your eyes and bluff. People are so risk averse. You nly heed Villain to fold 34% of the time to a half-pot bet for it to be profifable'in the long term. You can fail over half the time and still make money.

How often do you see someone 3-bet and barrel off? How often a6\youl'See’ Someone check-raise and barrel off? How often do you see someone Call an overbet with one pair? Almost never! People are very risk averse and you have to focus all of your attention to exploiting this factor.

The final idea is the following one. For a long time, poker theorists have Said that you don’t have much reason to bet for protection in NL. And they Were partially right. You don’t have much reason to use half-pot bets for Protection. But... if you incorporate 1/3- and 1/4- pot-size bets into your game it makes a lot of sense to start betting for protection, especially on Paired boards and in 3-bet pots.

There will be further discussion on this and more in the following material. For now you need to learn how to value-bet properly. Not the, “Oh TMmy god | hope he pays me off because I’m such a sick nit that I’m literally never bluffing in this spot” kind of poker. I'm talking about thick value. Let’s 9° to a little place called Value Town.

Value-betting

Value-betting is the most important skill you can learn in poker. You can’t

win without it. The good news for you is that 99% of live poker players are

underperforming !" this department. They leave a tremendous amount of

‘value on the table every session and don’t even realize it.

Calling Check-Raises

because nobody is actively looking to check-raise light.

Once again, let me remind you how important it is to understan4 the

. <i e Y 1 [| en ae a ee ere nm aly Villain, what is he thinking and what is he capable of ?”

Usually the answer is... “This Villain is an amateur who just got off wor, and wanted to unwind a bit by having a beer and watching the footba game at the table. I’m forced to assume that he has minimal comprehersion of solid pre-flop fundamentals because he just limp-called my isoletion raise. As such, it’s safe to assume that he has limited comprehension of fold equity and, even if he does, he’s not actively looking to put pressure on me.”

The rest of the time the answer is... “This Villain is a college dropout who is not disciplined enough to finish a degree and show up to work on time. He decided to give poker a go and gave himself the title of ‘profes sional poker player’ even though he has no long-term future in the game.

Villains such as these have a crippling psychological attachment a md Thus, they are incapable of check-raising with an optimal rang° ot hands.

By now it should be clear to you that poker is an extremely complex game. Calling Check-Raises with Straight Draws

Pro tip: Consider the size of future bets.

$5-S$10NL: Hero raises to $30. The Big Blind calls.

[221] 20230612_183903.jpg

gometimes you semi-bluff and face a raise in position. There are a lot fthings to consider.

What price are you getting? Are you drawing to the nuts? Will you get paid? Will you face another bet? How big will it be?

Here's one of the more interesting spots.

Villain checks. Hero bets $30. Villain raises to $90. Hero calls.

Hero c-bet with a double gutshot and got check-raised. He's getting 2-to-1 odds and it’s 4-to-1 against him improving on the turn. The good news is that he'll almost always be able to get stacks in if he makes his arid. Less disguised draws will often struggle to maximize value and that

must be considered.

[222] 20230612_183908.jpg

Villain bets $120. Hero raises to $880 all-in. Villain calls.

Hero made a very disguised draw against a very strong range of hands, This is one of the rare situations where he should raise the turn instead of waiting until the river. Any 9, 8, 7, 6, 5, 4, 3, or spade will kill his action on the river. He should shove and expect to get paid by two pair or better.

Floating to Stab

Pro tip: Float against people who c-bet and quit too Often,

$5-$10NL: The Cutoff raises to $30. Hero calls.

As discussed earlier, very few players double barrel at a high enough frequency on ace high boards. There’s a huge gap between their c-betting frequency and turn betting frequency on static textures. You should seek to exploit this by floating in these spots.

Villain checks. Hero bets $30. Villain calls.

most turns and evaluate rivers.

[225] 20230612_183926.jpg

villain checks. Hero bets $70. Villain folds.

I's almost impossible for Villain to check enough A-x to balance for githe useless Broadway hands in his c-betting range. Hero also picked up four more outs. Villain only needs to fold 12% of the time for Hero to break even, and that’s assuming Hero will never bet the river. Hero can make two very disguised straights and that will allow him to overbet against certain opponents. Betting is very clearly the play.

Pro tip: Bluff raise when you have numerous credible value combos.

$5-$10NL: The Cutorf ralses to $30. Hero calls.

range is very strong, and there are very few combos for you to bluff with.

Villain is probably c-betting with numerous Broadway hands that have no incentive to keep betting on any 8, 7, 6, 5, 4, 3, or 2. Hero also has two overcards and a backdoor flush draw. He should call and look to stab or bluff-raise on credible turn cards.

Villain bets $70. Hero raises to $225. Villain folds.

see this all the time. Villain will bet the Ri thn value, with no plan if he gets raised. The only straight combos in his range are 7-65, 6-55: 6-6, and A-6s. Meanwhile, there are dozens of weaker hands in his range: Hero has plenty of 6-x combos, pot equity and fold equity on this turn. He will also win Villain’s stack if he rivers a better straight. Bluff-raising this turn is an awesome, underutilized play.

Floating to Overbet

Pro tip: It’s best to overbet rivers against severely capped ran ges

$5-$10NL: The Button raises to $30. Hero calls.

Here's a line that’s been gaining popularity.

Hero checks. Villain bets $30. Hero calls.

Hero's check-call is multipurpose on this board. He has six pair + OESD Outs that are probably good if Villain checks the turn. He has six clean and two dirty straight outs. There are 10 Spades that give him a ton of equity: There are also 11 clubs in the deck that he could potentially represent on turns and rivers. There’s so much opportunity.

The overbet usually comes into play after the turn goes check-check.

Hero checks. Villain checks. Here’s where the magic happens...

Hero bets $240. Villain folds. Reasons for overbetting...

[232] 20230612_185257.jpg

Villain’s range is severely capped.

draws.

The best hand he could possibly have is A-10,

Most players are totally unwilling to make big river calls. Hero's range is uncapped.

He has many flush draws and K-Q combos.

It's really hard for him to be bluffing in this situation,

The only logical hands for him to bluff with are Q-9s, 9-85, and

used to bet half-pot in river situations like this. It was profitable. My opponents were folding well over 33% of the time. But one day | realized that | could force Villain to fold his entire range by overbetting. Why give him a chance to call with random A-x combos?

3-Bet Pots

We've looked extensively at 3-betting ranges haven't yet examined 3-bet pots. We now switch our attention to them. The biggest difference between single raised pots and 3-bet pots is the size of the ranges.

in single-raised pots, the opener should be using a very wide, depolarized range. In 3-bet pots the raiser should be using a much narrower, polarized range. As such, the need for balance is magnified in 3-bet pots, especially against thinking opponents.

Obviously, balance isnt terribly important against opponents who cal 3-bets too liberally. You just hammer, inane hammer until Villain surren- Gers and learns his lesson, But against thinking aS things become much more interesting.

“Ranges are sufficiently narrow so that if you're willing to apply yous ond and use some mental energy you can often count the exact number of combos in both ranges, That number gets smaller and smaller with each

bluffing frequencies and calling imc avait Lae eteatanicinae in real time.

[233] 20230612_185300.jpg

of mind. rhere’s also a psychological element in big games. In a vacuum, most 55-810 and almost all $1 O-$25NL players know how often they should be defending against river shoves. But... because many of them haven't poken their psychological attachment to money, they often deviate from what they know is optimal to avoid the pain of failure.

This is a basic evolutionary principle. Mammals have such a strong tendency to shy away from things that harm ther, that they will knowingly avoid things that benefit them if it creates exposure to pain. The easiest way to expose poker players to pain is to build pots early by 3-betting.

3-Betting Out of Position

Pro tip: Check to induce on ace high turns when 3-betting out of position.

$5-$10ONL: The Button raises to $30. Hero raises to $100. The Button calls

3-betting out of position can get you in a lot of trouble on dynamic boards, especially if you're playing 200bb+ err ‘Villain knows how to

leverage his stack. The good news is that you can use Villain‘’s own tactics

against him. This line doesn’t come up often but when it does it’s pure gold.

[234] 20230612_185307.jpg

Hero bets $100. Villain calls.

A competent Villain will defend against 3-bets in position with all pocket pairs, suited connectors, suited gappers, and suited aces when stacks are over 200bb. He doesn’t have to flop a set very often to break even, Villain can also put a tremendous amount of pressure on Hero if he isn’t 3-betting enough suited hands. His range will be capped at one pair on many boards and that is a huge liability.

Hero checks. Villain bets $300. Hero calls.

Check-shoving the turn would obviously be the best play if starting aren were $1,000. Villain could bet-call or bet-fold the turn with comb° raws and Hero would be indifferent. However, things change when stacks are $2,000. Hero's turn checking range appears to be K-K -10-10, Bre ay give-ups. Villain is obligated to stab the turn and follow through on the river with a huge range of hands.

Villain checks. Hero bets $135. Villain calls.

This is one of the rare situations where Hero should bet for thin value and protection. The number of combos that beat Hero is very small in comparison to the number of Broadway hands he should protect against. At most, Villain has 9-9, 4-4, 3-3, 10-10, and A-9 - 9-7s. That’s 35 combos ahead of Hero. Compare that to as many as 144 Broadway combos that have about 24% equity against Hero’s hand. There are also worse hands like 7-7,6-6, 5-5, 5-4s, and 6-5s that have to call at least one bet.

Villain checks. Hero checks.

check and evaluate the river.

Dact-Flop Play

[238] 20230612_185333.jpg

Villain bets $260. Hero folds.

This is why it's so hard to learn how to use a depolarized C-betting strategy effectively. All things considered, this is a pretty good runout fot Mero and it’s still tough to figure this situation out. As always, it’s best to start with pot odds.

Hero has to risk $260 to win $800 and is thus getting approximately 3-to-1 odds. In other words, he needs to have the best hand at least 25% of the time to make this call. Hero needs to deconstruct Villain’s range to estimate how often he has the best hand.

This process requires many assumptions because people use so many different approaches to flatting and defending against a squeeze out of the small blind. In my opinion, anyone who frequently flats out of the small blind should be treated as a fundamentally unsound player until proven otherwise.

always assume that Villain is flatting too often and defending against Hero's squeeze with 10-10 - 2-2/K-Qs - 5-4s — hands that can flop sets and big draws to compete against overpairs. [239] 20230612_185336.jpg

svercards and a gutshot or better. when Villain leads the river it’s important to consider what he’s trying oget called by. There are times when Villain will try to extract value from ce high but this isn’t likely to be one of those scenarios. The board is too <o-ordinated. | think Villain’s range is weighted toward A-J+. That makes his maximum value theshold 6-55, 9-9, 7-7, 4-4, 3-3 and A-J. That’s only 28 combos. So how many combos does Villain have to be bluffing with for Hero to break even? It’s just a simple algebra problem when Hero knows he needs to be right 25% of the time.

(Air Combos)/(Air Combos + Value Combos) = 0.25(10)/(10 + 28) = 0.26

Villain only needs to be bluffing with 10 combos for Hero to call. But here’s the problem: all of the hands in Villain’s range have some sort of showdown value. J-10, 10-10, 10-9s, 9-8s, 8-8, 7-6s, 6-6, 5-5 and 5-4s can all beat overcards at showdown. As a result, it isn’t likely Villain would elect to bluff with any of these hands.

There are only two ways Hero can justify a call on this river. The first is if he thinks Villain’s check-calling range on the flop is significantly wider. That would open up potential bluffing opportunities on this river. The second is if he thinks Villain could be value-betting with worse and hoping to get called by ace high. That's highly unlikely on this board texture.

“Altogether, it looks like Hero should fold in this spot. This is a great example of why | don’t recommend using a depolarized c-betting range. You truly have to be a world-class player to consistently make profitable

river decisions In spots like this. Sure, you can still bet for thin value and

protection, but do it sparingly, Try to avoid situations where soul-reading

is required to win.

lve coached 100+ poker students. Every single one of them eventualy asks me what to do on blank rivers like this. There is no cut-and-dry answer. This is one of the toughest spots in poker.

I's best to start by considering pot odds. Hero has to risk $800 to win $1,600 and is thus getting 2-to-1 on his money. He needs to be right 1 in3 times to break even. How do you know if he’s right 33% of the time?

Start by counting Villain’s value combos. Most players will value-bet AA, K-K, 0-0, - eel eS on this river. Occasionally you'll run into A-4s, 5-45, eee or A-Ds, You'll have to assign ql weight to each of these wild Card hands bonis they won't always be in Villain’s range.

ating Out of Position

$5-$10NL: Hero raises to $30. The Button raises to $100. Hero reraises to $250. The Button calls. Hero should 4-bet A-K. Calling the 3-bet allows Villain to realize most of his equity. It also makes it difficult for Hero to realize all of his equity. He's going to have to check-fold the flop about half the time. Why sacrifice equity by calling the 4-bet when he can generate fold equity by 5-betting?

Don’t fall for the trap. Villain checked the flop to minimize losses ang give Hero a chance to stab the turn. There’s no reason to attack on this board texture. Just surrender.

Villain bets $100. Hero calls.

used to raise in spots like this when | first started playing deep stack NL. | could get overcards to fold and still have equity against overpairs. It was profitable. But later | realized that calling is a way better option.

Why raise with a set when | could allow Villain to keep bluffing and/ or value-betting with worse hands? Why semi-bluff the flop when | have little incentive to raise with a set? Why not mimic the action | would take with a set and add credibility to my line?

[250] 20230612_185441.jpg

option for the same reasons as in the previous example.

Villain checks. Hero bets $1,600. Villain folds.

Most Villains don’t have the heart to fire a third barrel on blank rivers like this. They're happy to simply fold out some of Hero’s gutshots and A-x on the turn. Very few players go after Q-Q - 10-10 and 9-x combos on rivers like this. As a result, Hero can comfortably fold 8¥-7¥ to a river barrel and know he’s not getting exploited.

Now this spot gets really interesting when Villain checks the river. Most Villains never think to check the river with A-A and A-K. They’re terrified of missing out on value. That makes Villain’s range mostly air and Q-Q - 10-

used to bet $400 on this river. | was definitely generating more than 33% fold equity. But later when | started experimenting with overbets, realized | could fold out Villain’s entire range with a larger sizing. This line is extremely credible.

A competent Villain should realize that Hero still has 9-9, 6-6, 2-2, K-9s, and 59-49. Most Villains elect to check-fold Q-Q - 10-10 a Sia larger sizing. I've even seen some of them check-fold A-A and A-K. And why not? It’s the exact same line I'd take with a set...

03 - Post-Flop Play

[252] 20230612_185455.jpg

Then he has about 30 combos of K-K, Q-Q, sli 0, sila ana iad He also has about 24 combos of K-J and Q-J. His range is extremely vulnerable to turn and river barrels.

Most players check this flop with 7¥-7& and pray they have some sort of showdown value. They're afraid of getting called by A-x, K-K, Q-9, and J-x. So what if Villain calls? He's just building a bigger pot for Hero to win on turns and rivers.

Villain checks. Hero bets $200. Villain calls.

Hero will get a lot of folds on this turn card. Villain has to check-fold all of his K-K, Q-Q, and J-x combos that don’t have a diamond in them. It’s important to note that the jack on this flop is a diamond. It would be a totally different situation if the jack was offsuit and the four was a diamond. At that point, Hero would have to worry about Villain having flush combos.

Now think about the composition of Villain‘s check-calling range on the turn. He has a bunch of weak Broadway hands that probably have a diamond in them. This is one of the rare situations where Hero is actually hoping for a blank river card that will allow him to give Villain the bad pte

[253] 20230612_185458.jpg

Villain checks. Hero bets $400. Villain folds.

Now before you call me crazy, put yourself in Villain’s shoes. What does he beat? | guess you could say he beats offsuit K-Q, K-10, and Q-10 combos but that’s only if Hero is defending against a 3-bet with those hands. The hijack’s defense range versus the small blind should be quite a bit tighter than it would be if he was on the button.

Now how often do you see someone turn 7¥-7& into a multi-street bluff on this board? Almost never. That’s why this play is so effective. Villain is greedy. He isn’t checking A-x enough. His range is severly capped. Punish him.

4-Bet Pots

gyen in deep stack ens pet pots have very small continuance ranges. As the raiser, this drastically increases the importance of the three reasons to bet, the bet size that you use, and the street(s) that you choose 4 bet. As the caller, this drastically increases the importance of the orice you're getting to call, your hand classification, and what you're trying A accomplish against your opponent's range.

There are four things | see many people doing wrong in these situations both as raiser and caller. These mistakes are catastrophic because of the number of big blinds involved in the decision-making process. As a result, I've included extra hand histories in this section to really focus on these concepts. So please don’t think they’re redundant.

The first (and by far the worst) mistake that | see players making as the caller in 4-bet pots is shoving over the top of a c-bet to end the hand early. When you take a hand like J-J and shove over a c-bet ona low board, youre forcing Villain to play perfectly. Villain will fold all his worse hands and call with everything better. That is the exact opposite of your primary objective: allow Villain to make mistakes.

The second mistake that | see players making, as the raiser in 4-bet e i barreling with every bluff combo (A-K and air) on dry boards. A ot of people read some article on PokerNews and decide they're going © ry 4-betting, They don’t have enough experience in these situations to Nstruct @ reasonable barreling range so they c-bet, get to the turn, an Surrender. They do this over and over again.

4-Betting in Position

artificial intelligence programs like PokerSnowie have proven that 3-bet-

ting your entire continuance range out of the small blind will, in most cir. cumstances, be significantly more profitable than having a flatting range. used to be the only guy 3-betting K-J out of the small blind but now those days are over. I'm seeing more and more players implementing this strategy. The good news is that some of them are actually 3-betting too much,

$5-$10NL: Hero raises to $30. The Small Blind raises to $100. Hero 4-bets to $250. The Small Blind calls.

Wabsin should be 3-betting about 16% of the time versus button ont if he 3-bets more than 20% of the time, there's really no way for him profitably defend against 4-bets. So feel free to give the small blind the business if you start seeing him 3-bet hands like 1 Oo or A-80.

[257] 20230612_185517.jpg

he has to risk $1 400 to your ye20) ii he decides to 5-bet to asmaller size he'll be priced in to call with all but his weakest holdings. if Pitechiescto call he'll be out of position, ina bloated pot, witha bunch of weak holdings. How do those options sound? Sizing is key.

Villain checks. Hero bets $350. Villain calls.

This is one of the best possible flops to continue on. Hero's range is uncapped. He has K-K+ and A-K in his range. Most Villains will 5-bet all-in with those combos. Very few Villains will call with offsuit K-x combos.

So Hero is usually up against about nine K-x combos: K¥-Q¥, K#-Q&, Ke-Q¢, K¥-J¥, K&e-Je&, Ko-JO, KY-10¥, K&-10& and Ke-10¢.

Compare that to about 30 combos of Q-Q - 8-8 and a bunch of worthless Broadway hands. Hero must continue to apply pressure.

There are two betting patterns that can be used when the stack-topot ratio is 2.5-to-1. In cash games, usually c-bet about 65% of the pot and shove favorable turn cards. In tournaments, usually c-bet 30%, turn bet 40% and shove the river. Fold equity is the most important factor in cash games. Stack utility is the most important factor in tournaments.

03 - Post-Flop Play

[258] 20230612_185528.jpg

Villain checks. Hero bets $900 all-in. Villain folds.

This is one of the best possible turn cards for Hero. He isn’t risking $900 to win $1,200. He's risking $900 to win $2,100 because he has about 34% equity if Villain calls. Just take the total pot size and multiply it by Hero's equity to figure out his expected value when called: 34% of $3,000 is $1,020. Hero will net $120 even if Villain never folds.

Cold 4-Betting from the Big Blind

Pro tip: Consider throwing in a 4-bet bluff if Villain is 3-betting over 20%

$5-$10NL: The Button raises to $30. The Small Blind raises to $100. Hero 4-bets to $250. The Button folds. The Small Blind folds.

As discussed earlier, more and more pros are adopting the 3-bet or fold strategy out of the small blind. Many of them are 3-betting well over 20% of the time. It’s impossible for them to defend against a 4-bet at an appropriate frequency. Some of them know this and simply don’t care because nobody ever bothers to 4-bet them light.

Hero is risking $240 to win $140 in this situation. If both Villains fold 64% of the time, Hero could profitably 4~bet with any two cards. The cold 4-bet is such an underutilized move that this is often the case. It gets eve" better when you realize that Hero still has a decent amount of equity f called. Throw in the blocker effect and he can be printing money.

Having an ace in your hand makes it 25% less likely for Villain to rave] A-K and 50% less likely for him to have A-A.

[263] 20230612_185557.jpg

This weights Villain’s range toward air and increases the fold equity that Hero can generate. Moreover, it gives Hero at least 29% equity against K-K. Hero's equity goes up to 33% if he has a suited ace with wheel draw potential. It’s a lethal play when stacks are deep.

5-Betting Out of Position

Pro tip: Flatting a 4-bet with A-K (especially out of position), in a situation where you can 5-bet all-in for 3-5 times Villain’s 4-bet, is a terrible line that you should never take.

$5-S1ONL: The Button raises to $30. Hero raises to $100: Th utton 4-bets to $250. Hero 5-bets to $1,000 all-in. The Button c">

ero snould almost never flat out . rifice

fold equity. \t's a way better option.

[267] 20230612_185617.jpg

Hero's range is much wider and he might not be willing to 5-bet all-in if Villain is getting out of line. That's why it’s important to know the math behind the 5-bet.

it starts by estimating Villain’s calling range. In live cash, Villair’s calling range is almost always Q-Q+/A-K. Hero has 42% equity against this range. Use a fold equity calculator to determine how often Villain needs to fold for this shove to be profitable.

Villain needs to be folding 18% of the time for Hero to break even, Deconstruct Villain's 4-betting range and see how many cornbos he ects to fold for that to be possible. It’s easy to throw into a forrnula.

(Air Combos)/(Air Combos + Value Combos) = 0.18 5/(5 + 21) =0.19

Villain is calling off with 21 combos. He needs to 4-bet fold be ‘ne five combos for Hero to breakeven. Basically, Hero should shove if Villain ever 4-bet folds J-J or any other air type hands.

Now why is this better than calling the 4-bet? It's very simple. Calling © 4-bet allows Villain to realize most of his equity. It also makes It air" cult for Hero to realize all of his equity. He’s going to have to eheek-fold the flop about half the time.

Why sacrifice equity by calling the 4-bet when he can generate fold equity by 5-betting?

[268] 20230612_185623.jpg

5-Betting in Position

Live regs rarely 4-bet/fold when stacks are 100bb. Thus, you can have a 5-betting range at that stack depth. However, you should choose to flat your entire continuing range around 200bb. There are very few live pros willing to call off 150bb+ with less than K-K.

In fact, most of them will stop 4-betting Q-Q and A-K after seeing a 5-bet all-in for that many big blinds. They simply don’t want to deal with that kind of stack exposure. As a result, 5-betting at that stack depth becomes counterproductive.

You can flat 10-10+/A-Js+/A-Q and suited connectors if stacks are really deep. Flatting K-K+ insulates the rest of your range and makes you very difficult to play against. People have no idea if you have 5-4s or A-A.

Your range is uncapped on almost every board. Use that extra board coverage to generate fold equity in spots that most players can't target. You have so much more leverage that it is very difficult to profitably 4-bet me out of position when stacks are ultra deep.

100bb specialists fall for this trap every time. They have their little cookie cutter strategies for grinding 400NL on PokerStars. Put them '" 4 deep stack game and they crumble immediately, They don’t have enoug uations. Even worse, they have the heart, commitment, and mental fortitude to make a big call eat in the day, lose, and grind out of loss.

ADVANer:

[269] 20230612_185631.jpg

CLOSING WORDS

Pre-flop play is the foundation of post-flop profitability. It’s impossible to stay balanced if you play too many hands pre-flop. Your ranges will be too weak. Live players tried to speculate, online players tried to figure it using PokerTracker4, PokerSnowie tried to figure it out using artificial intelligence and | have simplified all of that data for you. Tight is right. Use the pre-flop ranges | have suggested. They are very tough to beat.

Never forget the four pre-flop profitability generators. Card edge is critical. You only get two cards. They need to be pretty good without the assistance of initiative, position, and skill edge. Constantly consider the implications of ignoring these edges. You will see the snowball effect of poor pre-flop decision-making in every session. This is where your profit comes from.

Do your best to avoid flatting out of the small blind. Why sacrifice all of your profitability generators without the assistance of pot odds? 3-bet with a tight range of hands that can defend against a 4-bet at an appropriate frequency, internalize the c-betting and barreling concepts that have been described inicbook: This strategy is heavily dependent upon your ability to balance a wider barreling range.

Closing Words

[270] 20230612_185635.jpg

uta. tha initiative and the protection of big pairs. play without the initiative and the protection of big pairs. Spend more time identifying the four types of opener,

Is Villain opening too wide or too tight?

Does he defend against 3-bets too often or not enough? How can you exploit that?

These factors will help you to create exploitative strategies. Polarized ranges, depolarized ranges, and flatting ranges can all be modified but only if you can identify how Villain is deviating from GTO play. You can use a similar process to construct 4-betting ranges.

How does Villain construct his 3-betting range? Is it polarized or depolarized?

Is it weighted toward value hands or bluffs? How can you exploit that?

When in doubt use a polarized 4-betting range. Utilize your blockers in combination with the 1/6th rule and you will be very difficult to beat. Never forget to consider the pre-flop dynamics as you advance to flop

What is your range? How does Villain perceive your range? As aresult, what is Villain’s range?

If you aren't sure, estimate the widest and narrowest Villains rang © and pick a happy medium, This process is critical on many lev ‘

[271] 20230612_185638.jpg

the initiative, count up your value combos, use the appropriate bluff-to-

[272] 20230612_185641.jpg

ing are constantly changing. It’s one giant game of rock, paper, scissors. You can throw rock every hand for months and crush the game if everyone is throwing scissors. But time and time again, your opponents will adapt and start throwing paper. Without a solid understanding of GTO play, you will fail to adapt and go broke.

The good news is that you have this book on your shelf. It’s like an insurance policy when times are tough. Never be afraid to take a step back and reevaluate. Poker is war, free enterprise, survival of the fittest, adapt or die, kill or be killed. It’s beautiful. Embrace it. Run good, have fun, and constantly look for ways to improve!
